head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Converts the 1-based rank to 0-based, so that rank 0 is the first permutation
(i−1)! = how many permutations share each choice of the next digit
Quotient = which block (which remaining digit), remainder = rank inside that block
Removes and returns the chosen digit so it can't be used again

p: `n = 3`, `k = 3` (the 3rd permutation, so 0-based k = 2):

There are n! permutations; generating them to reach the k-th costs O(n!). Each position's choice is determined by integer division by (i−1)!, so the answer is built in O(n²) (the `pop` shifts a list of at most n items).

60.takeaway: Factorial number system: divmod k by (i−1)! to pick each digit from the remaining list.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Fewest perfect squares that sum to i
Try every square not exceeding i as the last square used
Best for the remainder plus this one square

p: `n = 12`: the best last square for each i and the resulting count:

Taking the largest square first fails: 12 = 9 + 1 + 1 + 1 uses 4 squares, while 4 + 4 + 4 uses 3. DP tries all squares, so it finds the true minimum. (Lagrange's four-square theorem says the answer is never more than 4.)

279.takeaway: Coin change with square numbers as coins: dp[i] = 1 + min over squares j² ≤ i of dp[i − j²].

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Compresses the values to ranks 1..m so the tree is small
Array where tree[i] stores a count over a range of ranks; supports prefix counts and point updates in O(log m)
Counting items below a value dynamically
Moves to the next tree node responsible for index i (adds the lowest set bit)
Removes the lowest set bit: jumps to the previous block when summing a prefix
Scans from the right so the tree holds exactly the elements to the right of the current one

p: `[5,2,6,1]`, processed from the right (ranks: 1→1, 2→2, 5→3, 6→4):
For each x we need the number of already-seen (right-hand) values below it. A plain list would cost O(n) per query, O(n²) total; the Fenwick tree answers prefix counts and inserts in O(log n).

315.takeaway: Scan right to left with a Fenwick tree over compressed ranks; query the count of smaller values, then insert.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Exactly one bit is set: n is a power of two
0x55555555 is the bit pattern `0101…01`: it has 1s only at even bit positions (0, 2, 4, …), where powers of four have their single 1

p: Powers of two have one set bit at any position, but powers of four have it only at an even position (1, 4, 16, 64, …). 8 = `1000` has its bit at position 3, so the mask test fails and it is correctly rejected.

342.takeaway: Power of two (n & (n−1) == 0) whose single bit is at an even position (mask 0x55555555).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Tracking one end of an arithmetic progression
Gap between neighbouring remaining numbers (doubles each round)
The first element is removed when sweeping from the left, or when sweeping from the right with an odd count
Half the numbers are removed each round

p: After each round the remaining numbers form an arithmetic progression with a known step and count. Only the first element changes in a way that depends on the direction and parity, so (head, step, count) is enough: no list is ever built.

390.takeaway: Track (head, step, count) of the surviving arithmetic progression; no simulation of the list.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: F(0): the weighted sum with the original positions
F(k) = F(k−1) + (sum of all) − n · (the element that wraps from the end to the front)
Updating a sum in O(1) instead of recomputing

p: Rotating right by one shifts every element's index up by 1 (adding the sum of all elements to F) except the last element, which jumps from index n−1 to 0: it changes its contribution from (n−1)·x to 0, i.e. subtracts n·x in total once the +x is included. That gives F(k) = F(k−1) + total − n · nums[n−k].

396.takeaway: F(k) = F(k−1) + sum(nums) − n · (the element that wraps around).

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Drops the first and last character, removing the two trivial occurrences of s at positions 0 and len(s)
Substring test: s appears in the middle part only if s is built from a repeated block

p: If s is made of a block repeated, rotating s by the block length gives s again, so s occurs inside s + s at an offset strictly between 0 and len(s). If s is not periodic, the only occurrences of s in s + s are at offsets 0 and len(s), which the slice removes.

bullets: Time: O(n) with a linear substring search (Python's `in` is fast in practice and worst-case near-linear).

459.takeaway: A string is periodic iff it occurs inside (s + s) with the first and last characters removed.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: 1 divides every number; the number itself is excluded (a perfect number equals the sum of its proper divisors)
Only checks divisors up to √num; each divisor d pairs with num // d
A square root would be counted twice; add it only once
1 has no proper divisors that sum to it

p: `num = 28`: divisor pairs found:

blocks.h: Why stop at the square root?
p: Every divisor d ≤ √num has a partner num // d ≥ √num. Looping to √num finds both, in O(√num) instead of O(num).

507.takeaway: Sum proper divisors by pairs (d, n/d) up to √n and compare with n.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Reverses the usual order so that, within each level, the leftmost node is processed last
Order trick to avoid level bookkeeping
After the loop, `node` is the very last node dequeued: the leftmost node of the deepest level

bullets: The last node dequeued is 1: the bottom-left value.

p: BFS visits levels from top to bottom. Pushing the right child first makes each level come out right-to-left, so the last node of the last level is its leftmost one. No level counters or depth tracking are needed.

513.takeaway: Right-to-left BFS: the last dequeued node is the bottom-left one.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Every second element starting at index 0: the smaller element of each adjacent pair

p: Each pair contributes its smaller element, so the larger one is wasted. To waste as little as possible, the numbers wasted should be as small as possible, which means pairing each number with its closest neighbour in sorted order.

bullets: Space: O(n) for the sorted copy.

561.takeaway: Sort and sum every other element: pair up neighbours to waste the least.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Probability of ever reaching exactly score s
Sum of dp[t] over the last maxPts scores t < k: only those can still draw a card
From each previous score t (which can still draw) each card value has probability 1/maxPts
Scores below k can draw again, so they join the window
Scores more than maxPts back can't reach s: they leave the window
The game stops at any score ≥ k; the answer is the chance of stopping at a score ≤ n
The final score can't exceed k − 1 + maxPts, so n at least that is always safe

p: For `(6, 1, 10)` Alice draws once; scores 1–6 satisfy ≤ 6 out of 10 equally likely values: 0.6.
dp[s] needs the sum of up to maxPts previous probabilities. Recomputing the sum for each s costs O(maxPts); keeping a running window makes each step O(1), so the DP is O(n).

837.takeaway: Probability DP with a sliding-window sum over the last maxPts scores that can still draw.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Steps in the current side; it grows by 1 after every two sides: 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, …
if 0 <= r < rows and 0 <= c < cols: append
The spiral may leave the grid; only in-grid cells are recorded, but the walk continues

p: `rows = 1, cols = 4`, start (0, 0): the walk goes east, south (outside), west (outside), north, east …

The spiral is defined on the infinite plane; the grid just clips it. Stopping at the border would miss cells reached only after going around, so the walk continues until all rows × cols cells are found.

bullets: Time: O((max(rows, cols))²) steps, since the spiral may extend that far.
Space: O(rows × cols) for the output.

885.takeaway: Walk a growing clockwise spiral (lengths 1,1,2,2,3,3…) and record only the in-grid cells.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The smallest and largest numbers not yet used
An increase is guaranteed if the current value is the smallest remaining: everything after it is larger
A decrease is guaranteed if the current value is the largest remaining
One number is left at the end (lo == hi)

p: `s = "IDID"` needs 5 numbers 0..4:
bullets: After the loop `lo == hi == 2`, appended last: `[0, 4, 1, 3, 2]`.

blocks.h: Why does the greedy always work?
p: Taking the smallest remaining for 'I' guarantees the next number is larger, whatever it is; taking the largest for 'D' guarantees the next is smaller. The remaining pool is always a contiguous range [lo, hi], so the invariant holds at every step.

942.takeaway: Two pointers on the unused range: 'I' takes the smallest left, 'D' takes the largest left.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Letter counts of the first word
Counter intersection: keeps each letter with the MINIMUM of the two counts, dropping letters with 0
Expands counts back into repeated letters (a letter with count 2 is yielded twice)
Alphabetical order for a deterministic result

p: `["bella","label","roller"]`:
A letter is common to all words as many times as it appears in the word with the fewest copies. Intersecting counters one word at a time keeps the running minimum.

1002.takeaway: Counter intersection (&=) keeps the minimum count of each letter across all words.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The left half of the score: score = (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j) for i < j
Splitting an expression into a left and right part
Largest values[i] + i among positions before j
Running maximum of the left part
Best score for pairs ending at j
Updated after scoring j, so i < j always holds

blocks.h: Why can the pair be split?
p: The score values[i] + values[j] + i − j separates into a part depending only on i and a part depending only on j. Maximising over i for each j therefore needs just the running maximum of the i-part.

1014.takeaway: Score = (values[i] + i) + (values[j] − j): keep the running maximum of the first part.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of zeros: the extra length the duplicated array would have
`i` reads the original from the end; `j` writes into a virtual longer array
Only writes that land inside the real array are performed
Virtual array bigger than the real one
A zero is duplicated: it takes two slots

p: `[1,0,2,3,0,4,5,0]` has three zeros, so the virtual length is 11; the array after each step (pointers shown are the positions just handled):

Writing from the front would overwrite elements not yet read. Going backwards, the write position is always at or beyond the read position, so unread elements are never destroyed. That makes the O(1)-space in-place version possible.

1089.takeaway: Count zeros, then copy from the end into a virtual longer array, writing only positions < n.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of bits of the label = its level (level k holds labels 2^(k−1) .. 2^k − 1)
Smallest and largest label in the level
Mirrors the label inside its level: the label at the same position in the normal left-to-right order
Parent in a normal heap numbering
Collected from the node up to the root, so reverse

p: `label = 14` (level 4):

In a normal complete binary tree the parent of label x is x // 2. In the zigzag tree every second level is reversed, so the label at a position in a reversed level corresponds to the mirrored value lo + hi − x in the normal tree; the parent in the normal tree gives the parent's position in the level above (also reversed if that level is reversed, which the next iteration handles by mirroring again).

1104.takeaway: Mirror the label within its level (lo + hi − label) and halve it to get the zigzag parent.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The number as a string of digits
Replaces only the FIRST '6' (the third argument is the maximum number of replacements)

p: The leftmost digit has the highest place value. Changing the leftmost 6 to 9 raises the number the most; changing a later 6 increases it by less. If there is no 6 the string is unchanged.

1323.takeaway: Replace the first (leftmost) 6 with 9: str.replace with count 1.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Binary search for the FIRST position where x could be inserted: equals the number of elements strictly smaller than x
Counting smaller elements in a sorted list

p: With duplicates, `bisect_right` would also count equal values. `bisect_left` returns the index of the first occurrence, which is exactly the count of strictly smaller values.

1365.takeaway: Sort once; the count of strictly smaller numbers is bisect_left's index.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Subtract every node's value once for each parent: every non-root node is a child of exactly one node
What remains is the root's value (it is never subtracted); values are unique, so it identifies the node
XOR/sum trick for the unique unpaired element

p: Nodes given in shuffled order (root value 1; node 1 has children 3, 2, 4 and node 3 has children 5, 6):
bullets: The total ends at 1, the root's value.

p: A set of children would take O(n) space. The sum cancels every non-root value (added as a node and subtracted as a child), leaving the root. (XOR works the same way and avoids overflow concerns.)

1506.takeaway: Sum of all node values minus the sum of all children's values leaves the root's value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: How many times each distinct value occurs
Number of ways to choose 2 equal items among c copies: combinations C(c, 2)

blocks.h: Why a formula instead of a double loop?
p: Every pair of indices with equal values counts once. A double loop is O(n²); counting occurrences and using C(c, 2) is O(n).

1512.takeaway: Count occurrences and add C(c, 2) for each value.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Minimum deletions to make the prefix seen so far balanced (no 'b' before an 'a')
For a new 'a': either delete this 'a' (res + 1), or delete all earlier 'b's (bees)
A new 'b' never conflicts with earlier letters, so res is unchanged

p: `"aababbab"`:

blocks.h: Why do those two options suffice?
p: A balanced string is a's followed by b's. When an 'a' arrives after some b's, the string is unbalanced unless that 'a' is deleted, or every earlier 'b' is deleted (then all letters before it are a's). The cheaper option wins.

1653.takeaway: One pass: on 'a', res = min(res + 1, b's so far); on 'b', just count it.
